overview: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram, in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana, is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation — the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara (Medaram Jathara), held biennially in honour of the tribal mother-daughter duo Sammakka and Saralamma. Declared a State Festival in 1998, the Jathara draws 1.5–3 crore devotees over four days (next: 28–31 January 2028, with 2026 having just concluded), making it the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The rituals are performed entirely by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs (no Vedic or Brahmanic influence). Devotees offer 'Bangaram' (jaggery, equal to their weight in some traditions), 'Odi Biyyam' (sacred rice) and take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu (named after the tribal warrior Jampanna, who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream). The temple complex is administered by a non-hereditary chairman board, with MLA Santosh Chakravarthy having served as the first chairman (appointed 27 April 1968). The Telangana government reconstructed the altars of the deities (Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju, Pagididda Raju) at a cost of ~₹101 crore ahead of the 2026 Jathara, with additional ₹150 crore in development works.
summary: Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram (Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana) is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara — a biennial State Festival in honour of the tribal mother-daughter goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma. Held every two years in late January (next: 28–31 January 2028), the four-day Jathara draws 1.5–3 crore devotees, making it the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. Rituals are performed entirely by Koya tribe priests (no Vedic/Brahmanic influence). Devotees offer Bangaram (jaggery), take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu (named after the tribal warrior Jampanna), and worship the forest goddesses. The Telangana government spent ~₹101 crore on altar reconstruction and ₹150 crore on development works for 2026, deploying 21 departments, 42,000+ personnel, ~9,000 police, and ~500 NSS volunteers. Until 1955 only ~2,000 people attended, mostly Koya tribals; today the Koya community represents just 2% of the 1.3+ crore pilgrims.

history.content: Per tribal tradition, the goddess Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma were tribal leaders who lived in the 12th–13th centuries and led a revolt against the Kakatiya rulers' unjust tax on the tribal populace during a prolonged drought. Sammakka was married to Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas (who ruled the country of Andhra from Warangal City between 1000 AD and 1380 AD). She was blessed with 2 daughters and 1 son: Sarakka, Nagulamma and Jampanna respectively. Jampanna was a tribal warrior who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now named Jampanna Vagu after him; the water is reportedly red in colour — scientifically attributed to the soil composition, but tribally believed to be marked with Jampanna's blood). Per tribal legend, it was Sammakka's curse which caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. The Jathara commemorates their sacrifice and is the largest repeating tribal religious congregation in the world.
history.foundation_year: 13th century (per tribal tradition; legend dates back ~700 years)
legends: Sammakka was born ~6–7 centuries ago (13th century), when tribal leaders on a hunt found a newborn girl emitting enormous light playing amidst tigers; the head of the tribe adopted and raised her as a chieftain.
Sammakka married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma, Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna).
Sammakka led a tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax on tribals during a drought.
Her son Jampanna died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu); the water is still reddish — tribally believed to be marked with his blood.
Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule.
Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally, a small village near Medaram; Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (vermilion form).
The tribal goddesses are believed to 'visit' their devotees during the Jathara period; after 4 days, the goddesses return to the forest (Vana Pravesham).

history.content: Until 1955, only about 2,000 people visited Medaram, of whom the majority (1,500) belonged to the Koya tribe. In 1946, the Jatara was held with greater fervour and attendance than ever before under the supervision of Subedar Amir Ali Khan, who instituted multiple water stations, first-aid posts, mobile medical units, traffic regulation, sanitation, and crowd management — widely cited as a precedent-setting public welfare effort. Until 1998, the only way to reach Medaram was by bullock cart; in that year, the state government declared the 1,000-year-old festival as official (a State Festival) and laid down a motorable road. MLA Santosh Chakravarthy was appointed as the first chairman of the Sammakka Sarakka Temple on 27 April 1968. In 2008, ~8 million people attended; today attendance is ~10 million+ per cycle. The 2012 Jathara attracted ~1 crore people. The 2026 Jathara (28–31 January 2026) was the largest yet: an estimated 80 lakh devotees on the first two days alone, with the full 4-day total estimated at nearly 3 crore; the Telangana government deployed 21 government departments, 42,027 personnel, ~9,000 police officers, hundreds of CCTV cameras and 2 drone cameras, and ~500 NSS volunteers from Kakatiya University, Warangal. The government reconstructed the altars of Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju and Pagididda Raju at a cost of ~₹101 crore, with additional ₹150 crore in development works (parking, water stations, sanitation, medical camps, temporary bridges). The 2026 Jathara concluded at 7:55 PM on 31 January 2026 with Vana Pravesham (return to the forest).

sthala_puranam: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers, and was adopted by the head of the Koya tribe. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma and Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). When the Kakatiya rulers imposed an unjust tax on the tribals during a prolonged drought, Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma led a tribal revolt. Jampanna, Sammakka's son and a tribal warrior, died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu after him; the water is still reddish — tribally believed to be marked with his blood). Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. The forest goddesses are believed to 'visit' their devotees during the biennial Jathara, after which they return to the forest (Vana Pravesham) — the focal point of the four-day festival. The rituals are entirely performed by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs, with no Vedic or Brahmanic influence.
religious_significance: Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation and a State Festival of Telangana (since 1998). It is the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The temple is a non-Vedic, non-Brahmanic shrine entirely administered by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs. It is a major centre for tribal religious identity, drawing 1.5–3 crore devotees from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand. Devotees offer Bangaram (jaggery), Odi Biyyam (sacred rice), turmeric, vermilion, rice and cloth; women offer sarees; and pilgrims take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu. The temple is revered as a symbol of tribal resistance, women's leadership (Sammakka as a female warrior-chieftain) and forest-deity devotion. The 2026 Jathara was inaugurated by the Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy on 19 January 2026 (reconstructed shrine inauguration).
spiritual_significance: Devotees believe Sammakka and Saralamma are forest goddesses (Devathas) who 'visit' their devotees during the Jathara period and return to the forest after four days (Vana Pravesham). The rituals performed at the gaddelu (sacred altar) are believed to bestow protection, fulfilment of vows (Mokubadulu), and ancestral blessings. Devotees come seeking solutions to personal and family problems, court cases, marital issues, child-related concerns, and protection of tribal lands and forests. The red water of Jampanna Vagu is believed to remind tribals of the sacrifice of their gods and to induce courage in their souls. The festival is a major assertion of tribal cultural identity and continuity, and the journey to Medaram itself is considered a sacred pilgrimage.

miracles_and_devotee_experiences: Tribal devotees report that the red colour of Jampanna Vagu is attributed to the blood of Jampanna, the tribal warrior who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream — a story that has been transmitted for ~700 years.
Devotees report that prayers offered at the gaddelu (sacred altar) are answered in the form of fulfilment of vows (Mokubadulu).
Pilgrims describe the 'spiritual atmosphere, traditional offerings' and 'devotional atmosphere' as 'strong' even with lakhs of devotees attending (per Siasat 30 Jan 2026).
Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule — a long-standing tribal narrative.
The first chairman of the Sammakka Sarakka Temple was MLA Santosh Chakravarthy (appointed 27 April 1968), a fact recorded on the official commemorative board inside the temple premises.
architecture: The Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram has a distinct tribal-Shaivite architecture, blending folk-tribal elements with simple South Indian temple features. The gaddelu (sacred altar) is the focal point of the four-day Jathara, where the deities are ceremonially installed. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally (a small village near Medaram), and Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (a vermilion-form deity — i.e. the goddess is represented by a mound of vermilion rather than a stone or metal idol). The complex is in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt). The Telangana government reconstructed the altars of the deities (Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju, Pagididda Raju) at a cost of ~₹101 crore ahead of the 2026 Jathara. The Jampanna Vagu (a tributary of the Godavari) flows through the forest region, with a bridge constructed on top of it (Jampanna Vagu bridge). The complex includes Forest Tents (100 tents set up by the Forest Department; up to 5 persons per tent; 24-hour/12-hour rentals), Kalyana Katta, Ballon No. 5, and 21 government department-managed facilities.
architectural_style: Tribal-Shaivite architecture with simple South Indian elements; the deity Sammakka is a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (vermilion-form deity) rather than a stone or metal idol — a unique tribal feature. The altars were reconstructed for 2026.

timing_conflict_note: The Sammakka Saralamma Jathara is held BIENNIALLY (every 2 years) — the 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026, the next cycle is January 2028 (expected 26–29 January 2028). Outside the Jathara period, the temple is in the deep Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary and is not a typical daily-darshan shrine. JustDial lists '06:00 AM' opening hours for the temple listing (perhaps reflecting the Jathara's morning start). The 2026 Jathara was inaugurated by CM A. Revanth Reddy on 19 January 2026 (reconstructed shrine), with the main 4-day festival 28–31 January 2026, concluding at 7:55 PM on 31 January 2026. Each day of the Jathara has a distinct program (see 'darshan_timings' above).

sevas.name: Mokubadulu (vow fulfilment)
sevas.description: Devotees fulfil vows (Mokubadulu) by offering Bangaram (jaggery), Odi Biyyam (sacred rice), sarees, turmeric, vermilion and cloth to the goddesses. This is the principal offering at the Jathara.
sevas.charges: Voluntary; bangaram (jaggery) of a quantity equal to the devotee's weight is the most auspicious offering

sevas.name: Bangaram Offering (Jaggery equal to body weight)
sevas.description: The most important offering in the Sammakka Sarakka Jathara — devotees offer jaggery (bellam, called Bangaram) equal to their body weight to the goddesses. Symbolic of gold.
sevas.charges: Voluntary; quantity depends on devotee's choice

sevas.name: Odi Biyyam (Sacred Rice)
sevas.description: Women offer 'Odi Biyyam' (sacred rice) to the goddesses on Day 3 (the main offerings day).

sevas.name: Saree Offering

sevas.name: Punya Snanam (Holy Bath)
sevas.description: Devotees take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu, believed to be marked with the blood of the tribal warrior Jampanna. Considered central to the spiritual experience.

festivals.description: The principal and most significant festival — held biennially over 4 days in late January. The 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026; the next cycle is expected January 2028. Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, drawing 1.5–3 crore devotees over the 4-day period — the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The CM of Telangana (A. Revanth Reddy) inaugurated the reconstructed shrine on 19 January 2026; the 4-day festival itself was 28–31 January 2026, concluding at 7:55 PM on 31 January with Vana Pravesham. The 2026 Jathara deployed 21 government departments, 42,027 personnel, ~9,000 police, hundreds of CCTV cameras, 2 drone cameras, and ~500 NSS volunteers from Kakatiya University.
Tribal devotees perform small-scale pujas at the Kannepally and Chilakala Gutta shrines during Karthika Masam (off-Jathara period).
Per local tradition, the Jathara was historically associated with the full moon (Shuddha Purnima) day, though the modern 4-day Jathara runs Wednesday-to-Saturday in late January.

darshan_and_tickets.general_darshan: Free entry to Medaram and the gaddelu during the Jathara period. No entry ticket is required for the 4-day festival. Outside the Jathara period, the site is in the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary and is generally closed to non-tribal visitors (forest permits may be required for general visits).
darshan_and_tickets.special_darshan: No special darshan or VIP system is documented — the gaddelu is a shared, open platform where all devotees queue for darshan.
darshan_and_tickets.ticket_details: Forest Tent accommodation: ₹2,000 for 24 hours / ₹1,000 for 12 hours (contact: +91 95531 42346 — A. Venkat). All other offerings (Bangaram, Odi Biyyam, sarees, holy dip in Jampanna Vagu) are voluntary. The 2026 government spent ~₹101 crore on altar reconstruction and ₹150 crore on development works.

dress_code: Tribal devotees wear traditional Koya attire. For general pilgrims: traditional and modest attire is recommended — men often wear dhoti (and may remove the shirt at the inner sanctum / gaddelu per Telugu tribal convention); women wear sarees (which is also one of the principal offerings at the Jathara). Footwear is removed at the gaddelu and at the temple area. Pilgrims are advised to wear light, weather-appropriate clothing and to carry water during the crowded 4-day Jathara.

accommodation.availability: Accommodation is severely limited even on Jathara days — most pilgrims stay in Warangal, Hyderabad, or other nearby towns and travel in for the day. On-site: 100 Forest Tents (5 persons/tent); Airbnb options (per medaramjathara.com). The 2026 arrangements emphasised day-pilgrimage with massive bus operations rather than overnight stays at Medaram.
accommodation.booking_process: Forest Tent booking: contact +91 95531 42346 (A. Venkat) on the day or in advance. Airbnb: book via airbnb.co.in (specific Medaram listings exist). Most pilgrims travel from Warangal (~90 km) or Hyderabad (~300 km) for the day.
accommodation.first_come_basis: Forest Tents are on a first-come, first-served basis during the Jathara.
accommodation.price_range: Forest Tents: ₹2,000 for 24 hours / ₹1,000 for 12 hours (per 2026 official rates). Airbnb: variable, typically ₹1,500–₹5,000 per night for private homes around Medaram. Hotels in Warangal (the closest city, ~90 km): ₹800–₹4,000 per night for budget-mid-range.

best_time_to_visit: The 4-day Sammakka Saralamma Jatara in late January is the only time most pilgrims visit — next cycle January 2028 (expected 26–29 January 2028). For off-season visitors, October to February is the most pleasant weather window, though the temple is in the deep Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary and may be closed to non-tribal visitors outside the Jathara. Avoid peak days (Day 3 — Friday) if you dislike crowds (up to 40 lakh on the busiest day per 2026 arrangements). Pilgrims are advised to arrive early in the morning, carry water, wear light traditional clothing, and be prepared for significant walking and queueing.

travel.road: Medaram is ~90 km from Warangal city. Until 1998, the only way to reach Medaram was by bullock cart; in 1998, the state government laid down a motorable road. For the 2026 Jathara, TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily to move around 21 lakh people, with 30 bus points to Medaram. Special buses run from all areas of Telangana. From Hyderabad, the route is via Warangal; from Warangal, local buses and special Jathara buses. Buses also connect from Bhupalpally, Kothagudem, Mancherial, Karimnagar, and the surrounding districts. Massive parking areas are set up for the 4-day festival. The official website lists TGSRTC fares (e.g., Godavarikhani 175 km ₹400; Peddapalli 185 km ₹420; Manthani 150 km ₹350; B-Incline 175 km ₹400).
travel.rail: Nearest major railway station is Warangal (~90 km). Kazipet Junction is also a major railhead (~95 km). The Hyderabad + Greater Hyderabad regions together accounted for more than 5.18 lakh bus passengers during the 2026 Jathara, while Warangal zones and Karimnagar region also contributed significantly.
travel.air: Nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km, 5–6 hours by road).

Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary: at the temple site

travel_tips: The 4-day Jathara is held biennially in late January — the next cycle is expected January 2028 (likely 26–29 January 2028). Plan well in advance.
Day 3 (Friday) is the busiest day (up to 40 lakh visitors on the busiest day per 2026 arrangements). Choose Day 1 or Day 2 for shorter queues.
Wear traditional attire — men in dhoti (often shirtless at the gaddelu per tribal convention), women in sarees (which is also a principal offering).
Carry water, light food, comfortable footwear (which you'll remove at the gaddelu and Jampanna Vagu), and a towel for the holy dip.
Bring Bangaram (jaggery) of a quantity equal to your body weight for the principal offering — this is the most auspicious offering.
If you plan to take a holy dip in Jampanna Vagu, do so on Day 3 (the main day for snanams).
Avoid the area in the afternoon of Day 4 (Vana Pravesham) unless you specifically want to witness the return-to-forest procession.
Do not enter Medaram without a forest permit outside the Jathara period — it is in the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt).
Use the TSRTC special buses (4,000 daily) rather than private vehicles during the Jathara; the traffic jam can extend up to 60 km on the Warangal highway.
Take personal responsibility for your belongings — the crowds are massive (up to 3 crore over 4 days).
Use the missing persons camps at key locations if you get separated from family.
Be aware that there are no ATMs or banks at Medaram — carry sufficient cash.

introduction.en: Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram, in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary, Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana, is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation — the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara. Held biennially over 4 days in late January (next: January 2028), it draws 1.5 to 3 crore devotees, making it the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. Declared a State Festival in 1998, the Jathara is entirely performed by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs — no Vedic or Brahmanic influence. Devotees offer Bangaram (jaggery equal to their weight), take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu, and worship the forest goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma — a mother-daughter duo who led a tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax in the 13th century.

history.en: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka, Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). When the Kakatiya rulers imposed an unjust tax on the tribals during a drought, Sammakka and her daughter led a revolt. Jampanna died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu, with red-coloured water tribally believed to be marked with his blood). Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the Kakatiya decline. In 1946, Subedar Amir Ali Khan's stewardship set a precedent for public welfare. In 1998, the State Festival was declared and a motorable road was laid. MLA Santosh Chakravarthy became the first chairman in 1968. The 2026 Jathara deployed 21 government departments, 42,000+ personnel, and ~9,000 police, with ₹101 crore on altar reconstruction and ₹150 crore on development works.

travel_guide.en: Medaram is in the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), ~90 km from Warangal and ~300 km from Hyderabad. The 4-day Jathara runs Wednesday to Saturday in late January. The 2026 cycle was 28 to 31 January 2026, with the CM A. Revanth Reddy inaugurating the reconstructed shrine on 19 January 2026. The 4-day event concluded at 7:55 PM on 31 January 2026 with Vana Pravesham. TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily during the 2026 Jathara to move ~21 lakh people, with 30 bus points to Medaram. The nearest railway station is Warangal (~90 km); the nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km). For pilgrims: avoid Day 3 (Friday, the busiest, up to 40 lakh visitors), carry cash (no ATMs at Medaram), wear traditional attire (men: dhoti, often shirtless; women: sarees — also a principal offering), and bring jaggery (Bangaram) equal to your body weight. Outside the Jathara, the site is restricted due to the Wildlife Sanctuary.

faq.question: What is the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara?
faq.answer: It is a biennial tribal religious festival held in honour of the tribal mother-daughter goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma at Medaram village in Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana. It is recognised as Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, drawing 1.5 to 3 crore devotees over 4 days — the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. Declared a State Festival in 1998, it is performed entirely by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs (no Vedic or Brahmanic influence). The 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026; the next is expected January 2028.

faq.question: Where is the Sammakka Saralamma Temple located?
faq.answer: In Medaram village, Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana – 506344, India. The temple is in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), ~90 km from Warangal city and ~300 km from Hyderabad. The gaddelu (sacred altar) is the focal point of the Jathara; the Saralamma temple is in nearby Kannepally; Sammakka's 'Kumkuma Bharina' is at Chilakala Gutta.

faq.question: What is the schedule for the 4-day Jathara?
faq.answer: Day 1 (Wednesday) — Secret morning pujas at Kannepally; evening 6:00 PM: Saralamma brought to Medaram Gaddhe via Jampanna Vaagu; over 3 million devotees. Day 2 (Thursday) — Edurukolla Ghattam (bamboo-stick ritual); evening 6:00 PM: Sammakka brought from Chilakala Gutta to gaddhe; SP fires 3 gunshots to inaugurate the bali. Day 3 (Friday) — Main day: devotees take Punya Snanams in Jampanna Vaagu; main darshan of Sammakka and Saralamma; offerings of Bangaram, Odi Biyyam, sarees, turmeric, vermilion, rice, cloth. Day 4 (Saturday) — Final darshan; afternoon Ammavarlu Vana Pravesham (return to forest at ~6:00 PM); the 4-day Jathara concludes with religious chants.

faq.question: How big is the Sammakka Saralamma Jathara?
faq.answer: The 2026 Jathara drew an estimated 80 lakh devotees on the first two days alone, with the full 4-day total expected to reach nearly 3 crore. The Telangana government deployed 21 government departments, 42,027 personnel, ~9,000 police officers, hundreds of CCTV cameras, 2 drone cameras, ~500 NSS volunteers from Kakatiya University, and TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily. The traffic jam can extend up to 60 km on the Warangal highway. It is the largest tribal religious gathering in the world and the second-largest religious gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela.

faq.question: When is the next Sammakka Saralamma Jathara?
faq.answer: The 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026. The Jathara is biennial (held every 2 years), so the next cycle is expected January 2028 (likely 26–29 January 2028). The 4-day dates are finalized by the Pujari Association and conveyed to the Executive Officer of the Jathara.

faq.question: Who are Sammakka and Saralamma?
faq.answer: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers, adopted by the Koya tribe head. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma, Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). She led a tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax during a drought. Jampanna, her son, died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu). Per legend, Sammakka's curse caused the Kakatiya decline. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally; Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (vermilion form).

faq.question: What is the Jampanna Vagu?
faq.answer: Jampanna Vagu is a tributary of the River Godavari that flows through the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary near Medaram. It is named after the tribal warrior Jampanna (Sammakka's son), who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream. The water is still reddish in colour — tribally believed to be marked with his blood (scientifically attributed to the soil composition). A holy dip (Punya Snanam) in the red waters is central to the Jathara experience. The Jampanna Vagu bridge crosses the stream.

faq.question: What is Bangaram and how is it offered?
faq.answer: Bangaram is the local name for jaggery (bellam) — symbolic of gold. It is the most important offering in the Sammakka Sarakka Jathara. Devotees offer jaggery of a quantity equal to their body weight to the goddesses. The offering is part of the Mokubadulu (vow fulfilment) tradition. Other offerings include Odi Biyyam (sacred rice, by women), sarees, turmeric, vermilion, rice and cloth.

faq.question: How do I reach Medaram for the Jathara?
faq.answer: By road: ~90 km from Warangal (~2.5–3 hours); ~300 km from Hyderabad (~5–6 hours). TSRTC runs special buses during the Jathara from all areas of Telangana (30+ bus points to Medaram). By rail: nearest major station is Warangal (~90 km). By air: nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km). For the 2026 Jathara, TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily to move ~21 lakh people. During the Jathara, expect heavy traffic and plan for day-pilgrimage (most pilgrims stay in Warangal or Hyderabad and travel in for the day).

faq.question: Is there accommodation at Medaram?
faq.answer: On-site: 100 Forest Tents (₹2,000/24h, ₹1,000/12h, up to 5 persons/tent; contact +91 95531 42346 — A. Venkat). Airbnb private homes around Medaram (per medaramjathara.com). However, the official setup emphasizes day-pilgrimage from Warangal or Hyderabad. There are no ATMs or banks at Medaram — carry sufficient cash. Most pilgrims travel in from Warangal (~90 km) or Hyderabad (~300 km) for the day.

faq.question: What should I wear and bring for the Jathara?
faq.answer: Wear traditional attire — men in dhoti (often shirtless at the gaddelu per tribal convention); women in sarees (which is also a principal offering). Carry water, light food, comfortable footwear (which you'll remove at the gaddelu and Jampanna Vagu), a towel for the holy dip, and jaggery (Bangaram) of a quantity equal to your body weight for the principal offering. There are no ATMs or banks at Medaram — carry sufficient cash. Be prepared for massive crowds (up to 40 lakh on Day 3).

faq.question: What is the connection between the Jathara and Sammakka's curse on the Kakatiyas?
faq.answer: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. After Sammakka and her daughter led the tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax during a drought, and after her son Jampanna died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at Jampanna Vagu, the Kakatiya empire gradually declined. The Jathara commemorates this tribal resistance and the sacrifice of Sammakka, Saralamma and Jampanna. It is a major assertion of tribal cultural identity and the memory of the 13th-century tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya rule.
